components.name: Clock Dial
components.description: The signature component: bezel, a 60-position tick bezel (major every 5th), three dashed rain-intensity bands, the forecast fill, and hour/minute/second hands. Simplified here to a few representative ticks for the panel.

components.css: .ds-dial { width: 240px; height: 240px; } .ds-dial-rim { fill: none; stroke: #c1c7cd; stroke-width: 0.004; } .ds-dial-band { fill: none; } .ds-dial-band-light { stroke: #a6c8ff; stroke-width: 0.004; stroke-dasharray: 0.006 0.014; } .ds-dial-band-moderate { stroke: #4589ff; stroke-width: 0.005; stroke-dasharray: 0.018 0.012; } .ds-dial-band-heavy { stroke: #0043ce; stroke-width: 0.006; } .ds-dial-tick { stroke-linecap: round; } .ds-dial-tick-major { stroke: #161616; stroke-width: 0.014; } .ds-dial-tick-minor { stroke: #c1c7cd; stroke-width: 0.006; } .ds-dial-hand { stroke-linecap: round; } .ds-dial-hand-hour { stroke: #161616; stroke-width: 0.024; } .ds-dial-hand-minute { stroke: #161616; stroke-width: 0.014; } .ds-dial-hand-second { stroke: #0f62fe; stroke-width: 0.008; } .ds-dial-cap { fill: #ffffff; stroke: #0f62fe; stroke-width: 0.012; }

narrative.overview: Rain Clock reads as a well-made analog instrument that happens to know about rain, not as software wearing a clock skin. Everything on the dial — the bezel, the ticks, the hands, the intensity rings — belongs to the visual grammar of a real watch or barometer: thin metal, deliberate weight differences between major and minor marks, and restraint everywhere color could otherwise shout. The page around the dial stays out of the way: a quiet title bar, a quiet attribution strip, nothing that asks for a second look. This system explicitly rejects the conventions of a weather app. No numeric read-outs competing with the dial, no settings screens, no card grids of forecast data, no dashboard chrome. If a change would make this look more like software and less like an instrument, it's the wrong change.
keyCharacteristics: One signature surface (the dial) carries almost the entire visual identity; page chrome is minimal by design, not by neglect.
Two font stacks by role, not by accident: a light instrument face for anything drawn on the dial, plain system sans for page chrome.
Color is functional before it's decorative — blue only appears where it's telling you about rain.
Flat by default; the one shadow in the system is soft and ambient, never a card-style drop shadow.

rules.name: The One Accent Rule
rules.body: Instrument Blue (#0f62fe) marks the single live, moving element (the second hand). It does not spread to buttons, links, or backgrounds.

rules.name: The Two Blues Never Mix Rule
rules.body: Chrome accent blue and rain blue are different systems with different jobs — one says 'this is interactive/live,' the other says 'this is how much rain.'

rules.name: The Dial-Only Display Rule
rules.body: The light instrument face never leaves the SVG. Page chrome stays on the plain body stack.

rules.name: The Flat-Instrument Rule
rules.body: Nothing on the dial gets a drop shadow. Depth comes from line weight and layering, not elevation.

dos: Do keep every rain-intensity encoding doubled — color step and dash pattern — never color alone.
Do reuse Rain Fill/Rain Edge for anything else that represents 'the forecast' itself.
Do keep tick and hand stroke-width proportioned to their length.
Do give the quick-action icon buttons real default/hover/focus/active states before shipping more of them.
donts: Don't add menus, numeric read-outs, settings screens, or dashboard-style chrome.
Don't add card grids, drop shadows, or any 'lifted' surface treatment beyond the header's ambient separator.
Don't let Instrument Blue spread beyond the second hand into buttons, links, or backgrounds.
Don't hardcode new one-off spacing values outside the spacing scale.
Don't mix the display (dial) font into page chrome, or the body font into the dial.
